The fundamental difference between a drone and remote control device is that the drone can operate out of line of sight, autonomously or not.

This greatly expands the range of the drone relative to the operator's location and means if you see one flying around there's no guarantee that you'll be able to see the operator anywhere, whereas with traditional remote control devices, if you are near the device you are pretty much guaranteed to also be near the operator (and able to see them).

This has obviously upset and/or worried enough people to get the FAA to classify drones differently than traditional RCs.

Fascinatingly, the FAA rules that one must agree to when registering their drone stipulate that you will not fly it out of line-of-sight... so, if you have a camera on your drone, and were dreaming of sitting inside your apartment or car while it flew around and explored things... No longer allowed. This effectively eliminates true civilian-owned drones from American airspace altogether by requiring all drones to operate as traditional RC vehicles.

In my personal opinion, these regulations came about because previously, the technology to make true drones did not exist, and remote-controlled aircraft were expensive and (relatively) clunky: They were only operated by line-of-sight by a few people who had a significant investment in the craft, and were therefore more likely to be responsible, considerate, and careful with its operation.

With the advances in technology, now remote control aircraft can be operated outside of line of sight by everyone and their mother... and everyone and their mother is doing it. I will invoke Hanlon's Razor here: I don't think the FAA has any ulterior motives in this case, as unfortunate and frustrating as the new regulations may be.
